notes: \cpara{Introduces the post's one case, a pagan panelist's creation story. The story is the Norse one told in Snorri Sturluson's \textsc{Prose Edda}: the cow Audhumbla licks a man, Buri, out of salt-stones, and Buri's descendants Odin, Vili and Ve kill the giant Ymir and make the earth from his body. The post's summary matches it.}

\clogic{``Clearly'' stands where evidence would go, here and again two paragraphs on (``clearly had something to do with her knowing''). The one view on science the post reports from her is that religion and science are compatible.}
\cpara{The evidence for everything that follows: the author's impression of her manner. The author offers three names for it, each with a question mark.}

\cpara{Reports two things she said, and both fit a reading the post does not consider: that she took the myth as symbolic, not as history. She held that religion and science were compatible, and she explained the myth by the land the Vikings lived in. Wikipedia's article on Heathenry, citing academic studies, says most practitioners take the Norse cosmology as ``a poetic or symbolic description of the cosmos,'' and that few read Ragnar\"{o}k as ``a literal prophecy,'' though most, it adds, believe that the gods themselves exist. The post puts ``believed'' in quotation marks and does not report asking her what she meant by it.}
\cpara{Rules out Dennett's ``belief in belief'': she did not recite with ``fanatical faith,'' and did not act as if she needed the audience to believe.}

\cpara{Credits Dennett with suggesting that religious belief be studied as ``religious profession.'' I could not check this against Dennett's book. The students and Wulky Wilkensen reuse, as a hypothetical, the made-up writer of ``Making Beliefs Pay Rent (in Anticipated Experiences).''}

\cpara{Disagrees with Dennett, with a double hedge (``I think,'' ``may be slightly''). The support is a claim about ``most people'': that they are ``honest enough'' to repeat to themselves a religious statement they say aloud. No evidence is given for it.}
\cpara{Argues that ``profession'' does not fit either: someone professing to satisfy a priest, a fellow believer or their own self-image would pretend much more convincingly, and she did not try.}

\cpara{The thesis: the recital was ``cheering for paganism.'' The banner makes the difference between asserting and cheering easy to see. The post points to nothing she did that cheering explains and the other readings do not; the thesis rests on the impression of her manner in the second paragraph.}
\cpara{The analogy adds a second claim about her state of mind: that she believed ``she couldn't be arrested or criticized.'' No word or act of hers is cited for it.}
\cpara{Concludes that the absurdity was the point. The conclusion comes from the analogy in the previous paragraph, not from anything she is reported to have said.}
\cpara{The author's footnote: nothing is wrong with actually marching naked in pride parades.}
